THE SCIENCE BEHIND THE VIEW

Light takes the long way.

This is a view from an imagined camera near TON 618, not a telescope image or a reconstruction of its exact appearance.

What the renderer calculates

Light follows null geodesics in Schwarzschild spacetime. Precomputed light paths curve both the disk and background; captured rays form the shadow. Circular disk motion produces Doppler shifts and relativistic beaming, alongside gravitational redshift.

What we assume

A non-spinning black hole and a thin disk from 3 to 12 horizon radii. Orbit mode uses a static camera at 40 horizon radii; plunge mode follows a curved free-fall geodesic that loops nearly twice before capture, with energy E = 1 and angular momentum L = 1.9985 rₛ. Spin, disk geometry and orientation are not measurements of TON 618. The detailed orange disk and illustrative galaxy are procedural, inspired by NASA’s plunge film.

A scale, not an exact mass

We use approximately 66 billion solar masses, a commonly cited Hβ-based estimate from Shemmer et al. (2004), for scale. Mass estimates depend on the spectral method and have substantial uncertainty. At this mass, the non-spinning horizon radius is about 1,303 AU.

Time and color

Disk animation is accelerated by roughly 500,000×. Science mode uses a blackbody-inspired temperature profile and energy-shift shading, not a calibrated spectrum. Cinematic mode warms the palette and adds glow. The roughly 30-second plunge has accelerated, variable pacing and stops at 0.82 horizon radii. The camera’s own time is scaled to our TON 618 reference mass, so it spans many days. Use the 360° all-sky panorama to see every direction at once; its edges stretch like a world map. A perspective view is also available. Drag to look around or look back at incoming light. We do not model the singularity, plasma dynamics, or Kerr spin.

Explore the features

The shadow is larger than the event horizon: it includes directions whose light is captured. For a distant observer of this non-spinning model, the critical impact parameter is √27 / 2 horizon radii.

NASA’s reference film depicts a 4.3-million-solar-mass black hole. This independent real-time approximation keeps TON 618’s reference mass and does not reproduce the supercomputer renderer. Finite lookup resolution smooths the smallest photon subrings. The photon sphere is a physical orbit at 1.5 horizon radii; the apparent bright ring is a lensed image, not a solid object.
